reasoning.notes: Most play decisions rest on specific, correct inferences: which special cards are already gone, what a rival's bid implies they will or will not play, and how many tricks each opponent still needs. Bids are sometimes generic hand counts, but play-time reasoning regularly tracks the remaining cards and uses the opponents' trick needs as a weapon.

evidence.quote: Both Pirates are now out, so seat 3's Pirate wins this trick whatever I play. That makes the Mermaid unbeatable in the last trick
evidence.shows: Card counting turns the Mermaid into a sure winner, which later earned the +40 capture.

evidence.quote: my Escape will safely lose the last trick, because both Escapes are accounted for (mine and the one Seat 3 played)
evidence.shows: Tracks the played cards to confirm a guaranteed loser.

evidence.quote: leaves my Y3 for the last trick. Then seat 1 or seat 2 will likely be forced to take a trick they don't want
evidence.shows: Reads both rivals' trick counts and gives up 10 points to set them, which matches the designer's idea of forcing rivals over their bids.

evidence.quote: Seats 1 and 3 both bid 0, so they want me to take tricks and will dodge whenever they can.
evidence.shows: Uses the public bids to predict how opponents will play.

planning.notes: Within each 3-trick hand, players routinely order their cards: they keep a sure winner, lead a loser into opponents who still need tricks, and set up forced last-trick plays. Cross-hand planning is limited to final-hand score arithmetic, and the 3-trick horizon caps how deep plans can go.

evidence.quote: I then lead B1 on the last trick. Each opponent will have only one card left, so they cannot choose to dodge.
evidence.shows: A two-trick plan that relies on opponents being forced on the last trick; it worked.

evidence.quote: Seat 2 wins this trick and leads trick 2, so I play third and see both cards before choosing.
evidence.shows: Gives up a trick to gain position for the later tricks.

evidence.quote: I then lead my Escape into the last trick. Seat 1 and Seat 3 each have one card left, so one of them will almost certainly win it.
evidence.shows: An endgame plan to make the leader's 0 bid fail.

evidence.quote: this gives me 140. If I take all three tricks, seat 2 takes none.
evidence.shows: A last-hand bid chosen from the scores, as the designer anticipated.

luck.notes: With 3-card hands, holding the Skull King, the Pirates or the Mermaid largely decides who can bid high and collect bonuses, and some hands were lost to an unseen special card. The exact-bid scoring and 9 hands soften this but do not remove it.

evidence.quote: There is about a 36% chance that none of these is in the opponents' 6 cards.
evidence.shows: A strong hand's bid of 3 was broken by the Skull King in an opponent's hand.

evidence.quote: With B4, a Pirate and the Mermaid, I expect to win most or all tricks.
evidence.shows: A dealt power hand set up the eventual winner's early lead.

weak_spots.what: Seat 3 bid 3 and then led the Pirate into an unseen Skull King, giving away the trick and a +30 capture. Seat 2 had reasoned in hand 1 that leading the Mermaid first avoids giving that bonus away, and the Mermaid would also have beaten the Skull King.
The reasoning is muddled ('I hold the Mermaid's place already used'). The conclusion that only a Pirate or the Skull King beats B5 was right, but it rested on garbled card tracking.

Seat 1 bid 3 counting on seat 2 dropping to 110. A seat 2 bid of 1 with 0 tricks only falls to 120, so the line needed seat 2 to bid 2 or more, and this went unexamined. Seat 1 noticed it only at turn 73.

summary: Winning rewards real reasoning: counting cards, reading bids and steering rivals over or under their bids. Players do this well, though deal strength still decides a fair share of results; longer hands or more cards per hand would deepen planning beyond the 3-trick horizon and dilute the effect of who holds the few special cards.
